info.bio:
Blur es el nombre de una banda inglesa de Britpop. Llamada Seymour en un principio, el nombre se adoptó por orden de la discográfica. Blur se formó en Londres en 1989 por Damon Albarn (vocalista, tecladista, guitarrista), Graham Coxon (guitarrista) y Alex James (bajista). Posteriormente, el batería Dave Rowntree se unió a la formación.
Blur fue una de las bandas británicas que aparecieron en el inicio de la caída del grupo británico The Stone Roses, mezclando psicodelia pop rock con fuertes guitarras.

scenes.name: Brit-pop y post-pop
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Como tantas veces, el fenómeno más publicitado es el menos interesante: un «brit-pop» de grupos terriblemente parecidos y tediosos, sin apenas imaginación. Lo anticipan Lightning Seeds, La's, Teenage Fanclub y Heavenly; estalla con Boo Radleys, Blur (Parklife) y Oasis (el «farol» que mejor personifica la moda). Suede y el glam-pop (Super Furry Animals, Placebo), las excepciones de High Llamas (Hawaii) y Supergrass, el revival mod (Ocean Colour Scene, Wildhearts), Elastica, Sleeper, las Spice Girls; Trembling Blue Stars, Tindersticks, Delgados. El post-pop de Radiohead, «la banda más publicitada y sobrevalorada de la década», cuyo OK Computer es una obra maestra del falso vanguardismo; Coldplay, Travis.

mentions.author: Piero Scaruffi
mentions.text: …the bands destined to rule the world (according to the British press of the time): the Boo Radleys (1), who turned "retro" with Giant Steps (1993), Blur, who attained stardom with Parklife (1994), and Oasis, the band (or the "bluff") that best personified the fad, from the exuberant Definitely Maybe…

podcast.title: Early History and Manchester Association - 1989
podcast.body: Blur first appeared around 1989, originating from Colchester, East of London. Despite their geographic origin, they were often mistakenly associated with the Manchester scene due to their early sound, which featured "Manchester-ish bits" in songs from around 1991. "They had first serviced back in 1989 and although they were from Cold Chester, which is East of London, they were lumped into what was happening in Manchester in the Northwest, some 300 kilometers away."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Early Financial Struggles (1992)
podcast.body: Despite releasing a well-selling debut album, touring extensively, and playing successful concerts, Blur found themselves completely ruined and deeply in debt by mid-1992. This situation, now seemingly unthinkable, was a common problem due to "shameful" record contracts of the era, which also affected bands like The Smiths, who despite many albums and concerts, earned very little.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Dominant British Bands (End of 1994)
podcast.body: By the end of 1994, Blur was one of three bands dominating the British music scene, alongside Oasis and Suede, indicating an impending explosion in the Britpop movement. "As we got to the end of 1994, three bands dominated the British music scene. There was Oasis, there was Blur, and there was Swade."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Rise to Prominence (1994)
podcast.body: By 1994, Blur had established themselves as one of the most important new bands in the UK, becoming a key act in the Britpop movement. "by 1994 they were one of the most important new bands in the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: "The Battle of Britpop" Winner (August 1995)
podcast.body: Blur emerged victorious in the direct chart showdown against Oasis in August 1995. By moving "Country House" to release on the same day as Oasis's "Roll With It" (August 14, 1995), Blur sold 274,000 copies, surpassing Oasis's 216,000 and claiming the number one spot. "Blur, the winners of the epic Britpop showdown of August 1995."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Brit Pop Rivalry with Oasis (1995)
podcast.body: Blur's rivalry with Oasis escalated into a "Record War" in August 1995, representing the peak of Brit Pop. This intense competition involved "Brit Pop's two biggest stars going at each other's throats," starting with a near-fight at a San Francisco radio station and an almost-brawl between Damon Albarn and Liam Gallagher backstage at an award ceremony. Damon Albarn deliberately moved up Blur's new single release date to clash with Oasis's, setting the stage for a nationwide sensation where all music papers, magazines, and daily papers covered the battle, and bookmakers even took bets on which single would achieve the number one spot. "The Blur versus Oasis Record War, with the height of Brit Pop in August of 1995."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 7

podcast.title: Early Career Weariness (1995)
podcast.body: By 1995, Blur was described as being "burnt out" after four or five years in the market, having released several albums, faced various economic issues, and grown quite disillusioned with the recording industry. "Blur llegaba a 1995, ya relativamente quemado, 4 o 5 años en el mercado había sacado varios iscos, había estado ya con varios temas económicos, había estado bastante desencantado con aiscografica."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: El BRIT POP como negocio discográfico

podcast.title: Fatigue and Disillusionment (1995)
podcast.body: By 1995, as Britpop reached its peak, Blur, despite their success, arrived with a different attitude compared to fresh, younger bands like Oasis. They were fatigued from extensive touring, tired of record label pressure (specifically from EMI), disillusioned with the music industry, and experiencing internal problems, feeling like "old dogs" in the movement.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Initiation of "Battle of Britpop" - August 15, 1995
podcast.body: Damon Albarn deliberately escalated the rivalry with Oasis by moving the release date of a new Blur single ("Country House") to August 15, 1995, the exact same day Oasis was releasing their single ("Roll With It"). This move triggered a massive media frenzy and the iconic "Battle of Britpop." "Damon Alborn started it. When he found out when Oasis was going to release the first single from their What's the Story Morning Glory album, he moved the release date of the new Blur single up to the very same date, August 15th, 1995."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: The Chart War of August 1995
podcast.body: Blur strategically scheduled the release of their single "Country House" for August 14, 1995, the same day Oasis was releasing "Roll With It." This intentional clash sparked the "Battle of Britpop," captivating the entire UK, with bookmakers even laying odds on the outcome. "But then Blur announced that they too would release a single called Country House on that very same day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Veteran Status in Britpop Battle (1995)
podcast.body: By the time of the "Great Britpop Battle" in 1995, Blur possessed a veteran status, having already navigated early career struggles, stylistic shifts, and financial difficulties. This experience made them less eager to fully participate in the media-fueled rivalry compared to the younger, more pressured Oasis. "Blur que habían empezado antes y ya habían tenido sus problemas, sus tumbos se habían arruinado, ya eran un poco perro viejo."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Trainspotting Soundtrack Contribution (1996)
podcast.body: Blur contributed to the first *Trainspotting* soundtrack in 1996. This soundtrack gained widespread acclaim and is often listed among the best movie soundtracks of all time, known for its mix of old and new rock and electronic music that captured the film's desperate yet uplifting tone. "New Order, Pulp, Blur, Underworld, Elastica, Lou Reed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Damon Albarn's Aesthetic Reversal (1997)
podcast.body: By 1997, Damon Albarn underwent a "stunning aesthetic reversal," shifting his musical interests from proudly British pop (anti-grunge) to low-fi American alternative bands (Pavement, The Pixies), obscure 1970s German progressive rock, and Sub-Saharan African music. He also began spending more time in Iceland, manifesting this change in Blur's self-titled 1997 album. "Damon had become fascinated by low-fi American alternative music from bands like Pavement and The Pixies. He was also getting deeper into obscure German progressive rock from the 1970s and several forms of music from sub-Saharan Africa."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Graham Coxon's Departure (Pre-2003)
podcast.body: Guitarist Graham Coxon was asked to leave the band before *Think Tank*'s release due to a "bad attitude" and for "stopped showing up to recording sessions." His absence meant the end of the original Blur lineup. "By this time, guitarist Graham Coxon had been asked to leave the band. Apparently he had a bad attitude and he had stopped showing up to recording sessions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Think Tank (2003) - Listening Insights
podcast.body: Re-listening to Think Tank provides insight into the album's characteristic lack of guitars due to Graham Coxon's absence, his minimal contribution on "Battery in Your Leg," and the album's overarching dual themes of anti-war pacifism and hedonistic partying. "escucharlo otra vez y ver por un lado porque no hay guitarras porque el garras en coxon no estaba, escucharlo el último drummer in Giorlès que es la queñísima contrapación que llamaba el garras en coxon al disco y escuchar esas dos temáticas entre el disco tequejas, no a la guerra pacifismo, me voy de juerga."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Blur - Think Tank y su dificil grabación.

podcast.title: Think Tank (2003) Singles Artwork
podcast.body: The singles released from Think Tank (referred to as "los indios" in the transcript) featured artwork with similar themes to the album cover, though these were created by other artists and graphic designers, not Banksy. "Los indios que salieron con el disco todos tienen en sus portadas temáticas muy similaresa a esta pero ya no las hizo más que sino que las hicieron otros artistas y diseñadores gráficos."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Blur - Think Tank y su dificil grabación.

podcast.title: Think Tank (2003) Tour - Absence of Graham Coxon
podcast.body: The tour supporting Think Tank was described as somewhat melancholic due to the absence of Graham Coxon, who was a significant contributor, especially given the album's overall lack of prominent guitar parts. "La gira fue un poco triste porque no estaba en cocción que siempre aportó mucho y leches un disco planeante no tienen guitarras."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Blur - Think Tank y su dificil grabación.

podcast.title: Alex James – Became Celebrated British Cheesemaker After Blur's 2004 Hiatus
podcast.body: When Blur's extended hiatus began in 2004, bassist Alex James moved to the Cotswolds and immersed himself in artisan cheesemaking. His farm features more than 400 sheep, valued for their milk. His specialty is a soft goat's cheese wrapped in a vine leaf called "Little Wallop," and he also makes varieties called "Geronimo" (named after his eldest son), "Churchill Lady," "Rotten Bastard," and "Mad Bitch," plus a triangular variety he calls "Wedgie." He produced a video series called "The Cheese Diaries" for *The Guardian*. The origin of his cheese obsession traces to an early Blur Japan tour when, asked what fans should bring him as gifts, he drunkenly said "cheese" — and was deluged with Japanese cheese at every subsequent visit. "Alex became, in the words of some, the poster boy for the renaissance of British cheesemaking."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Breakup Date (October 1, 2004)
podcast.body: This date is assigned as when "the blur that everyone knew had stopped functioning." "As far as I can tell, the blur that everyone knew had stopped functioning by October 1st 2004."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Reunion Rumors and Attempts (2004-2008)
podcast.body: During the hiatus, there were "all these rumors" about Blur getting back together, including "meetings, lunches, and even some aborted recording sessions." "But in the background, there were all these rumors that Blurr, proper blurr, would get back together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Reunion Confirmation (December 9, 2008)
podcast.body: Blur officially confirmed their reunion on this date, announcing plans to play shows in 2009. "But it wasn't until December 9th of 2008 that there was any kind of confirmation about anything. That's when Blurr said, okay, it's true. We are getting back together. We're going to play some shows in 2009."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Reunion Gigs Begin (June 2009)
podcast.body: The band started performing reunion shows in June 2009. "And they did starting in June."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Advocacy for Space Exploration and Beagle 2 Project
podcast.body: Deeply interested in space, Alex James became an active campaigner for funding the Beagle 2 probe to Mars, particularly when the European Space Union began universe exploration. He convinced Blur to compose a song for the probe, which was intended to be the first rock band broadcast from Mars, though the probe was unfortunately lost upon landing in 2003. "He began campaigning to anyone and everyone for funding of a probe to Mars called Beagle 2."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alex James' Diverse Interests and Education
podcast.body: Alex James initially studied French in college, where he first met the other members of Blur. Beyond his musical career, he cultivated strong passions for space exploration and cheese. He later pursued formal education in science, earning an honors degree in astrophysics from the University of Bath after two years of study. "He went to college to study French."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alex James's Astrophysics Studies and Residency at Oxford
podcast.body: During Blur's extended hiatus, Alex James dedicated two years to studying astrophysics at the University of Bath, where he earned an honors degree. Following this, he was appointed artist in residence in the astrophysics department at the University of Oxford. "During Blur's lengthy and maybe permanent break, Alex spent two years at the University of Bath studying astrophysics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alex James's Award-Winning Cheese Production
podcast.body: After Blur achieved significant financial success, bassist Alex James moved to the countryside, acquiring a farmhouse on 200 acres populated by hundreds of sheep and cows, which he transformed into a cheese-making operation. His cheeses have earned numerous awards and are widely available in British supermarkets. Notable varieties include "Blue Monday" (named after the New Order song), a creamy Shropshire blue cheese, as well as "Queen Maud," "Rotten Bastard," and "Mad Bitch." Alex James is highly regarded in the cheese industry, having served as a judge in competitions and authored books on the subject, including "All Cheeses Great and Small." Even the Royal Family is said to enjoy products from his farm. "Alex is so good at cheese that he has been a judge in cheese competitions."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alex James's Cheesemaking Career
podcast.body: Alex James, the bass player for Blur, is also a master cheesemaker. His farm is located in the Cotswolds in the UK, and he named a private road on his property "Steven Street" to honor producer Steven Street, who produced albums for Blur, The Cranberries, and The Smiths. "His farm is in the Cotsweld in the UK on a road he calls Steven Street. In honor of producer Steven Street, who produced albums for Blur, The Cranberries, The Smiths and many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alex James's Consultation on European Space Agency's Mars Express Mission (Beagle II)
podcast.body: Alex James consulted on the construction of Beagle II, the British component of the European Space Agency's Mars Express Mission. The probe was launched from Kazakhstan on June 2nd, 2003, with an intended landing on Mars around Christmas Day of the same year. It was supposed to play a song written by Blur upon landing, but the mission failed, and the probe was declared lost. "Alex asked, and he was allowed to consult on the craft's construction."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alex James's High-End British Cheese Making
podcast.body: Alex James runs a farm in the Cotswolds where he produces high-end British cheese. He also contributes a column on cheese making for a major London newspaper and hosts tasting events for the public. "He's got this farm and the cut swalls. He makes some very high-end British cheese."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alex James's Lifestyle
podcast.body: Bass player Alex James was noted as "a boozer and a drugie." "It also didn't help that bass player Alex James was a boozer and a drugie."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Alex James's Membership in British Astronomical Association
podcast.body: Alex James, the bass player for Blur, has been a long-standing member of the British Astronomical Association for many years, indicating his deep interest in space and astronomy. "He's been a member of the British Astronomical Association for years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alex Roundriegud Borden's Pursuit of Law
podcast.body: Drummer Alex Roundriegud Borden went off to law school during the band's hiatus. "drummer Alex Roundriegud Borden. He went off to law school."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Anti-Grunge Stance
podcast.body: Damon Albarn was reportedly very upset about British kids wearing flannel shirts, symbolizing the American grunge invasion, and was jealous of Suede's success in carving a niche. He decided Blur would fight back with a British approach. "Another guy who was really upset about all those British kids wearing flannel shirts was Damon Albart of Blur."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Artist in Residence at University of Oxford
podcast.body: Since January 2007, Alex James has held the esteemed position of artist in residence at the University of Oxford. "And since January of 2007 he's the artist in residence at the University of Oxford."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Artistic Sensibility
podcast.body: Blur is mentioned among a group of bands that possess an inherent artistic sensibility without being "over the top," often attributed to members having attended art school, studied art, or collected art. "You too, the cure, Marilyn Manson, Roxy Music, the Sex Pistols, Blur, they all get it without going over the top, mainly because each one of them either A went to art school, or B studied art, or C collect art."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Franz Ferdinand: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Band's Involvement in Space Exploration
podcast.body: In 2003, Blur composed a call sign for the Martian probe Beagle 2. The probe was intended to broadcast a special instrumental, a nine-note composition loosely based on the Fibonacci sequence and named "Far Out," upon landing to signal its operational status to Earth. Unfortunately, Beagle 2 was lost, but it was later speculated that it did survive the landing and played the song, though its damaged antenna was pointed incorrectly, preventing the signal from reaching Earth. "In 2003, the band composed a call sign for a Martian probe called Beagle 2."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Bowie's Appreciation for Blur
podcast.body: David Bowie was a known fan of Blur, acknowledging their importance in the alt-rock era. This mutual respect between Bowie and the new generation of musicians demonstrated his continued engagement with contemporary music. "Knowing that Bowie was a fan of the pixies and Irvana and the smashing pumpkins and swayed and a wasis and blur and vice versa, you had to give him respect."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Breakup and Reformation
podcast.body: Blur broke up for a while after Britpop's decline but later reformed for "big money." "Blur broke up for a while before reforming for big money."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Brit-Pop Peer
podcast.body: Blur is mentioned as a contemporary Brit-Pop band, characterized by a "faster, more movement, more agile, more fun" British style, contrasting with Pulp's more "kitsch" approach. Pulp was also noted for escaping the Brit-Pop movement in a similar fashion to Blur. "if Blur was that more agile, more movement, more agile, more fun British, and Oasis was that more classic British movement of Paul Weller and the Rolling Stones, if The Jam, then Pulp was that more kitsch movement."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Brit-Pop Revolutionaries
podcast.body: In 1991, Blur, described as very young, played a pivotal role in revolutionizing British pop music. Their emergence marked a shift in focus for the recording industry, which then oriented itself towards this new generation. "ya en 1991 unos jovencísimos Blood y Basis revolucionaban el pobre tánico."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: La generación perdida del Indie: SHOEGAZE

podcast.title: British Astronomical Association Member
podcast.body: Alex James holds a membership in good standing with the British Astronomical Association. "He's a member in good standing with the British Astronomical Association."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Britpop Movement (Mid-to-Late 90s)
podcast.body: Blur was a key band in the Britpop movement, which was a British response to American Grunge. "the British were still ringing out what they could from Britpop...you know Oasis and Blur and Elastakund swayed in all those bands."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Britpop Rejection
podcast.body: Blur became "really, really tired of the whole Brit pop thing" and sought a completely new musical direction. Graham Coxon, deeply immersed in the American indie scene and lo-fi bands like Pavement, advocated for this change, which the band embraced for their self-titled album. "See, Blur was really, really tired of the whole Brit pop thing and they wanted to do something completely different."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Britpop Success on Tiny Label
podcast.body: Blur achieved mainstream success during the mid-1990s Britpop scene while signed to Food, described as a "tiny little label." This illustrates how independent artists in the UK could penetrate the mainstream due to the unique characteristics of the British music industry. "People forget that blur made it big while on a tiny little label called Food."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Britpop's First Couple Connection
podcast.body: Damon Albarn's relationship with Justine Frischmann of Elastica, who was also a former member and girlfriend of Suede's Brett Anderson, was widely covered, leading the media to dub them Britpop's "official first couple." "Britpop now had an official first couple."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Co-creator of Gorillaz
podcast.body: Damon Albarn, a member of Blur, co-created the virtual band Gorillaz with cartoonist Jamie Hewlett. "Gorillas, the virtual band created by Blur's Damon Albarn and cartoonist Jamie Hewlett."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Trying to be a Superstar in the 21st Century

podcast.title: Creative Struggles in Post-Madchester Era
podcast.body: Prior to embracing Britpop, Blur experienced creative difficulties, feeling "stuck in some kind of post-madchester funk which just wasn't working" and struggling to find their niche while Suede gained traction. "Blur continued to struggle creatively. They were stuck in some kind of post-madchester funk which just wasn't working."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Damon Albarn's Aesthetic Reversal
podcast.body: By 1997, Damon Albarn had a change of heart regarding the proudly British music he had championed against foreign grunge. He became fascinated by low-fi American alternative music (Pavement, Pixies), obscure 1970s German progressive rock, and Sub-Saharan African music, spending less time in London and more in places like Iceland. "By 1997, he'd had a change of heart."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Damon Albarn's Anti-Grunge Stance
podcast.body: Damon Albarn was openly critical of grunge's popularity in the UK and "upset about the appearance of flannel shirts on British shores," stating his mission was to "get rid of grunge" much like punk aimed to get rid of hippies. He advocated for people to "smarten up" and be more energetic. "If punk was about getting rid of hippies, he said, then I'm getting rid of grunge."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Damon Albarn's Departure
podcast.body: Damon Albarn "had left blur behind" to create Gorillaz, indicating a transition in his musical focus. "Damon Alburn had left blur behind..."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: Damon Albarn's Diverse Projects
podcast.body: Singer Damon Albarn was highly active during Blur's downtime, working with Gorillaz, another band called The Good, The Bad, and The Queen, and exploring Middle Eastern and African music, even writing a Chinese opera. "while singer Damon Albarn was busy with guerrillas and another band called The Good, The Bad, and The Queen. He also got deep into Middle Eastern and African music. And yeah, there was that Chinese opera he wrote."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: Damon Albarn's Motivation for British Sound
podcast.body: After a particularly bad tour of America, Damon Albarn was determined to make British music distinctly British again, reacting to a UK music scene dominated by American sounds. This resolve directly led to the creation of "Park Life." "Damon Alborn of Blur had a lot to do with this. After a particularly bad tour of America, he came home to a country that was a wash in American music and he became determined to make British music British again."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Damon Albarn's Ping Pong Fandom
podcast.body: Damon Albarn is an admirer of ping pong. "He's a ping pong fan too."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Damon Albarn's Relationship with Noel Gallagher
podcast.body: Damon Albarn was referred to as Noel Gallagher's "once-mortal enemy," implying a significant past rivalry, particularly in the context of Liam Gallagher criticizing Noel for associating with him. "Damon Albarn of Blur."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Damon Albarn's Solo and Reunion Careers
podcast.body: Damon Albarn pursued an important solo career and also reunited with Blur, which had led to doubts about the future of the Gorillaz project before its eventual strong return. "de Imon Albanha había retomado su carrera con Blur, estaba teniendo una carrera importante en solitario y todos teníamos muchas dudas de que esto fue se ha pasado y vuelve con muchísima fuerza."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: David Rowntree's Astronomy Hobby
podcast.body: Blur drummer David Rowntree owns a telescope and dedicates many hours to observing the night sky. "Blur drummer David Rountry is his own telescope. He spends hours looking up at the night sky."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Entry into Britpop (Late 1980s)
podcast.body: Blur began working very early, almost in 1989, and quickly started releasing music. Their early presence in London, a city not then a major hub for new bands like Manchester or Scotland, positioned them perfectly as labels in the city were actively seeking new talent.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Early Struggles with Alcohol
podcast.body: After a strong start, Blur faced early difficulties, stumbling "hard in a haze of alcohol" before getting their act together. "Blur came out of the gate hard, but then they stumbled hard in a haze of alcohol."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: European Guitar Production Example
podcast.body: The more guitar-heavy parts of Blur's music serve as a prime example of the 90s European approach to guitar production, characterized by distinct and dry sounds. "Tienes ese ejemplo de las partes más guitarras de Blur, que son como un nuevo grande referente entre ajo de guitarras que aquí agraja un coxon."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Mellon Collie and The Infinite Sadness: ¿Por qué suena diferente?

podcast.title: Fans Dancing to Electronic Music
podcast.body: Fans of Blur were among those observed dancing to The Chemical Brothers at rock festivals, a previously unimaginable occurrence in the early 1990s that highlighted the groundbreaking crossover appeal of Big Beat. "gente que escuchaba o así o que escuchaba a Blur o que escuchaba a PULP y que de repente estaban bayando a los chemical brothers."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: The Chemical Brothers. Padres de la cultura BIG BEAT

podcast.title: Featured on Big Shiny Toons 2
podcast.body: Blur was included on the *Big Shiny Toons 2* compilation CD by Much Music in 1997. This album, which highlighted 100% alt-rock tracks, sold more than 1.2 million units in Canada, reflecting the strong market for alternative music. "featuring the prodigy, blur, Marilyn Manson, Bush, Collective Soul, the Tea Party, Radiohead, Stone Temple Pilots, and more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 2

podcast.title: First Band to Put Music on Mars
podcast.body: In conjunction with the European Space Agency's Mars Express mission, Blur recorded a special instrumental call sign for the Beagle 2 lander. Although the mission failed upon touchdown and the transmission was never received by Earth, it is possible the piece was played, making Blur the first band to put music on Mars. "Whatever the case, Blur was the first band to put music on Mars."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Gradual Rise to Stardom
podcast.body: In contrast to Oasis's rapid ascent, Blur underwent a multi-year progression to achieve their superstar status. Their journey involved evolving from Madchester influences to eventually embracing and defining the Britpop sound. "Blur que estuvieron años de progresión hasta ser unas grandes estrellas."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Iconography of Britpop
podcast.body: Blur, particularly with their album "Modern Life Is Rubbish," heavily incorporated classic British iconography into their promotions and album art. This included images of the Union Jack, Doc Martens boots, and Fred Perry polos, reflecting a growing obsession with British symbols that became characteristic of Britpop.

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Influence on Cranberries' Album Art
podcast.body: Blur's recent photoshoot, which featured the band members posing in suits, directly influenced The Cranberries' decision to adopt a similar style for the cover of their 1994 album, "No Need to Argue." This choice aimed to achieve a stark and unified look. "Everyone is in suits because blur at just recently posed for a photo the same way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Stories Behind Iconic Album Covers Part 2

podcast.title: Influence on Damon Albarn's Music
podcast.body: Touring the world with Blur exposed Damon Albarn to various musical genres, which he wanted to explore further. However, Blur itself was not the ideal vehicle for these new influences, leading to the creation of Gorillaz as an experimental outlet. "Damon says that touring the world with blur brought him to contact with all kinds of music. He wanted to fiddle with these new influences, but blur wasn't really the place to do that."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: International Act at Edge Fest
podcast.body: Blur was among the international acts added to Edge Fest throughout the 1990s, alongside bands like Foo Fighters and Green Day. Their inclusion helped diversify the festival's lineup, though Edge Fest primarily remained a Canadian event. "International acts were added throughout the decade, including the food fighters and blur in Green Day."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of the 90s CanRock Explosion

podcast.title: Interviewed by Host
podcast.body: Blur was among the artists interviewed by the host over the years. "I've had the privilege of talking to a ton of really cool people over the years...Morrissey Blur."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Introduction of British Nationalism
podcast.body: Blur played a pivotal role in reintroducing a new British nationalism and the celebration of British customs into the musical landscape. This cultural and musical stance set a precedent that Oasis later adopted, albeit with influences rooted in even more traditional British rock. "Blur que había introducido ese nuevo nacionalismo británico, esa nueva exaltación de las costumbres británicos a la música otra vez."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Journalism and Media Career
podcast.body: Alex James diversified his career by writing for various British newspapers and magazines. He also made appearances on British television, including "University Challenge," and engaged in other TV and radio work. "He began to write for several British newspapers and magazines."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Krautrock Fan
podcast.body: Damon Albarn, a member of Blur and Gorillaz, is described as a "huge crop rock fan," implying that his musical creations are significantly shaped by these German influences. "Damon Albarn of Blur and Gorillaz is a huge crop rock fan."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Manayerti's Role in Calming Tensions
podcast.body: The tense initial reunion of the band members was somewhat mitigated thanks to Manayerti, who is described as a great friend of the group and helped to soothe the situation. "gracias a Manayerti, siempre ha sido un gran amigo del grupo, se siguió un poco solentada."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Blur - Think Tank y su dificil grabación.

podcast.title: Misattribution as Manchester Band
podcast.body: Despite originating from Colchester, Blur was often "thrown on the pile" and categorized as a Manchester band by some due to the influence of the Madchester sound and similar musical characteristics in their songs. "Blur, a band from Coldchester originally, we're thrown on the pile."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Modern Elements in Style
podcast.body: For a period, Blur adopted modern elements in their style, demonstrating the lasting impact of mod culture and its aesthetics on subsequent artists. "Oasis had modern elements to their style as did blur for a while."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Name Change to Blur
podcast.body: The independent label Food convinced the band to change their name from Seymour to Blur, a decision that preceded their rise to prominence. "They convinced them to change their name to Blur."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Original Name "Seymour"
podcast.body: The band initially performed under the name Seymour before attracting the attention of the indie label Food. "Then there was a group called Seymour, who attracted the attention of an indie label called Food."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Overall Album Sales Disparity
podcast.body: Despite winning the single chart battle, Blur's album "The Great Escape" sold significantly less than Oasis's "(What's the Story) Morning Glory," selling "a little more than a tenth" of Oasis's 25 million copies. At the 1995 Brit Awards, Blur received no trophies, while Oasis won three. "The great escape sold a little more than a tenth of that. At the 1995 Brit Awards, Oasis won three trophies and Blur got none."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pavement's Influence
podcast.body: Blur, specifically their late 90s work, was identified as a group influenced by Pavement, demonstrating the lasting impact of Pavement's Lofi indie rock sound. "Pavement's influence would later be heard in the music of late 90s blur, and also groups like Modest Mouse, Spoon, and The Walkman."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Plagiarism Accusation from Boys Keep Swinging
podcast.body: A song by Blur was accused of plagiarizing "Boys Keep Swinging" from David Bowie's *Lodger*, as referenced by Damon Albarn. "una de las canciones de Blur que estaba acusada de haber plagado por Skipshing in, que es una de las canciones del Lodger."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: David Bowie: La trilogía de Berlin 3

podcast.title: Post-'13' Hiatus and Solo Projects
podcast.body: After recording the album '13', Blur members separated to pursue independent projects before reuniting for 'Think Tank'. "Lord se juntara después de separarse la grabación del 13 para seguir proyectos independientes."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Blur - Think Tank y su dificil grabación.

podcast.title: Post-Breakup Reunion
podcast.body: Blur managed to resolve their internal differences and eventually reunited, joining a significant wave of bands from various eras who got back together in the 21st century. This reunion trend was often driven by the financial opportunities presented by live touring amidst declining CD sales. "So did the smashing pumpkins and blur and even the stone roses managed to hold it together for six years starting in 2011."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 1: (100-91)

podcast.title: Post-Britpop Breakup and Reunion
podcast.body: Following Britpop's decline, Blur "broke up for a while before reforming for some big money," indicating a temporary hiatus before a financially motivated reunion. "Blurr broke up for a while before reforming for some big money."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Post-Feud Reconciliation
podcast.body: Following the breakup of Oasis in 2009, the animosity between Blur and Oasis members began to subside. Damon Albarn and Noel Gallagher have since mellowed with age and have performed together on stage, acknowledging their shared experiences of the 1990s without focusing on past conflicts. "Age has meld both Noel and Damon to the point where they've performed together on stage."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Madchester Creative Funk
podcast.body: After the Madchester scene declined, Blur struggled creatively, finding themselves stuck in a "post-magester creative funk" that wasn't working for them. This led Damon Albarn to adopt a new mission statement for the band. "They were stuck in some kind of post-magester creative funk, which just wasn't working for them or anyone else for that matter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Publicity from Anti-Grunge Comments
podcast.body: Damon Albarn's vocal opposition to grunge generated significant positive press in British music papers, contributing to the burgeoning Britpop movement in the winter of 1993-1994. "This made for some very good press in the British music papers."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Recording at Abbey Road Studios
podcast.body: Blur is among the list of legendary artists and bands who have made albums at the historic Abbey Road Studios in London. "I mean, Beatles, Pink Floyd, Oasis, Blur, Muse, Kate Bush, DePeshmo, Iron Maiden, Queen, You Tube Michael Jackson, Glenn Miller. They all made albums there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Stop Me If You've Heard This One Before

podcast.title: Relationship Breakdown
podcast.body: Justine Frischmann and Damon Albarn broke up, primarily due to drug problems, ending the "Britpop first couple" pairing. "Meanwhile, Justine and Damon Oliver broke up mostly over drug problems."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Renowned Cheese Maker
podcast.body: Alex James has established himself as one of the most respected cheese makers in the United Kingdom. "He's now one of the most respected cheese makers in all of the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rivalry with Oasis
podcast.body: What started as a friendly rivalry mushroomed into a full-on war with Oasis, culminating in a direct chart battle in August 1995. Blur was characterized as the "articulate defenders of the realm and diaries of modern British culture, middle class, slightly posh from London." "In one corner, blur, articulate defenders of the realm and diaries of modern British culture, middle class, slightly posh from London."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Rivalry with Oasis - "Death Match"
podcast.body: As Blur cleaned up their act, they became pitted "head to head with Oasis as the leading British band," leading to a fierce "death match" rivalry. This was one of the most vicious rivalries in British music history. "By the time Oasis got rolling, blur had cleaned up their act to the point where they were pitted head to head with Oasis as the leading British band. And the result was nothing short of a death match."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock: Chapter 12

podcast.title: Separation due to Creative Differences
podcast.body: Blur experienced a separation due to significant creative differences between Damon Albarn and Graham Coxon, which led them to pursue different paths. "como no pasamos paso con Blur que de Inmanal van a ir a en coxon tenían importantes diferencias creativas que llevan a disolver la banda."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Vuelven los Smashing Pumpkins... mas o menos

podcast.title: Single Chart Victory
podcast.body: On August 20, 1995, Blur's "Country House" won the chart battle against Oasis's "Roll With It," selling 274,000 copies to Oasis's 216,000, a margin of 58,000 units. This victory earned Blur the number one spot and an appearance on "Top of the Pops," where bassist Alex James wore a torn-up Oasis t-shirt. "But all the record sales were tallied up and the results were released on August 20th, 1995. The winner was Blur. 274,000 copies to 216,000 copies, a 58,000 unit margin of victory."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Son Named Galileo
podcast.body: Alex James named his son Galileo, a personal detail that reflects his enduring fascination with astronomy and scientific figures. "Oh, and did I mention he has a son named Galileo?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Strategic Timing Post-Cobain's Death
podcast.body: Blur released their album *Park Life* 17 days after Kurt Cobain's death, fortuitously positioning themselves "in the right place, at the right time, with the right album" to fill the void left by grunge's decline and capitalize on a shift in musical tastes. "The 17 days after Kurt died, Blur released a career altering and game-changing, not to mention a very British album called Park Life."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rise and Fall of Britpop

podcast.title: Tense Reunion in London
podcast.body: The band's reunion for 'Think Tank' began with a tense meeting in a London studio, as the four members had not seen each other for a long time. This initial gathering was described as quite tense and disjointed. "Se juntan en Londres en la estu grabación y no se habían visto en muchísimo tiempo. Entonces esa primera reunión de ley, los cuatro, fue bastante tensa y bastante coja."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Blur - Think Tank y su dificil grabación.

podcast.title: The Battle of Britpop with Oasis
podcast.body: Blur and Oasis, both emerging in the mid-1990s, engaged in an intense rivalry, fueled by class, authenticity, and media attention. In February 1995, Blur won four Brit Awards and publicly suggested they should share awards with Oasis. Later, Damon Albarn attended an Oasis number one party for "Some Might Say" to congratulate them but was met with Liam Gallagher's bragging. The feud was intensified by a rumor of Damon Albarn's one-night stand with a girl Liam Gallagher was seeing. "One of the greatest and most intense was the fight between Oasis and Blur in the middle 1990s. This was definitely real and undeniably ugly."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: The Good Mixer Hangout
podcast.body: In the early and middle 1990s, The Good Mixer pub on Inverness Street in Camden, London, became a frequent hangout for members of Blur. They, along with other Britpop figures, would often get "stupid drunk" there. This pub was a central hub where many bands formed and songs took shape during the Britpop era. "Guys from blur and oasis got stupid drunk there many times."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Shrines ｜ From the Archives

podcast.title: Time Apart (4 years, 2 months, 8 days)
podcast.body: Blur was apart for this approximate duration, calculated from October 1, 2004, to December 9, 2008. "If we use those two dates, October 1st 2004 and December 9th 2008, blurr was a part for four years, two months and eight days."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Reunions: Some Lasted....and Sadly, Some Didn't ｜ Part 1

podcast.title: UK Vinyl Editions
podcast.body: Blur's records were available on vinyl in the UK, demonstrating the country's commitment to the format during a period when most of the world had abandoned vinyl production. "de Blur."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan

podcast.title: Undervalued Original Cassette
podcast.body: The original cassette of a Blur album (referred to as "Manses" by the speaker, likely a phonetic transcription of an actual album name like *Modern Life Is Rubbish*) was acquired for a remarkably low price of 50 cents. This illustrates how, despite the rising interest, many cassettes remain undervalued in certain markets, offering opportunities for collectors to find bargains. "yo tengo el caseto original de blur mancés de de ver en caset y para que 50 centimos por ella."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
